title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 05–06
description: Advanced workplace language for colleagues, collaboration, shift patterns, job satisfaction, remuneration, benefits and employment conditions, with register and usage contrasts.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-provided Cambridge book. Target expressions were selected by checking both teaching pages, exercises and answer keys; Portuguese translations, notes and illustrative sentences were independently written rather than copied from the book.

audit.scope: Units 5 and 6 teaching sections, numbered vocabulary glosses, the Unit 6 Language help box, exercises 5.1–5.5 and 6.1–6.5, and their answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is included for individual words where confidently established; longer expressions have a blank IPA rather than speculative connected-speech transcriptions.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing package text, examples, explanations, headings and notes are in English; Brazilian Portuguese is restricted to pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the two study pages and their facing exercises with the relevant answer-key pages, including illustrated glosses and the Language help warning. Checked sense, register, typical collocations, prepositions and Portuguese translations. Performed programmatic checks of JSON schema, required fields, ID uniqueness, provenance, word audio targets and example completeness. Browser import, live synthesis and speech recognition were not tested.
audit.limitations: No MP3 recordings are included. Static validation does not establish successful browser import, actual TTS pronunciation or speech-recognition behaviour. Leave and redundancy terminology describes UK English and may not correspond to legal rules in other countries.

units.title: Unit 05 — At work: colleagues and routines
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 16–17 (PDF pages 18–19).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Work and study · colleagues, professional relationships and work routines
learningObjectives: Distinguish counterparts, opposite numbers, workmates and colleagues in professional contexts.
Explain collaboration, rapport, job-sharing and hot-desking using appropriate work-related collocations.
Contrast routine and rewarding work through nuanced adjectives such as mundane, monotonous, mind-numbing and stimulating.
Discuss shifts, workload, career limitations and self-employment using idiomatic British English expressions.

sectionsChecked: A · Colleagues: annotated expressions and numbered glosses
B · During the day: four work-pattern accounts and their numbered glosses
Exercises 5.1–5.5, including the adjective matching exercise

items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: I still consult former colleagues when I encounter an unfamiliar technical problem.
items.note: Neutral or professional term for someone who works in the same organisation or profession.

items.pt: colega que exerce função equivalente em outra unidade ou organização
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: Our opposite numbers in Berlin manage the same systems as we do in São Paulo.
items.note: Someone holding a corresponding position elsewhere; more precise than simply colleague.

items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: They maintained a constructive working relationship despite their disagreement.
items.note: Use a good, close, effective or strained working relationship, not work relationship.

items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: Day-to-day collaboration between engineers and researchers has improved reliability.
items.note: Day-to-day modifies recurring routine activity; collaboration is generally uncountable.

items.pt: profissional ou representante em posição equivalente
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: She discussed the rollout with her counterpart at the overseas subsidiary.
items.note: A more formal synonym of opposite number, also used for equivalent objects or institutions.

items.pt: estabelecer uma boa sintonia ou relação de confiança
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: A new team leader must establish a good rapport without avoiding difficult conversations.
items.note: Rapport denotes mutual understanding and ease; the final t is silent in British English.

items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: Her rapport with the technicians made complex negotiations easier.
items.note: Uncountable; often build, establish or have rapport with someone.

items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: Rather than waiting for instructions, he took the initiative and proposed a test plan.
items.note: Fixed expression: take the initiative, not make the initiative.

items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: A strongly hierarchical organisation may discourage junior staff from raising concerns.
items.note: Describes structures with ranked levels of authority; compare hierarchy.

items.pt: hierarquia informal de poder ou prioridade
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: Everyone understood the pecking order, even though it was never written down.
items.note: Often implies status-based priority, not just a formal organisational chart.

items.pt: divisão de um mesmo posto de trabalho entre duas pessoas
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: A job-share allowed both specialists to continue working part-time.
items.note: Typically two people share the responsibilities of one full-time position.

items.pt: sistema de mesas compartilhadas sem postos fixos
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: Hot-desking saves office space but can make teamwork less spontaneous.
items.note: An office arrangement in which employees use available desks rather than permanent assigned ones.

items.pt: colega de trabalho, geralmente de modo informal
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: Several workmates invited her to dinner after her first week.
items.note: Informal, especially British; colleague is usually more neutral or professional.

items.pt: conviver socialmente com colegas fora do trabalho
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: I occasionally socialise with workmates after conferences.
items.note: British spelling socialise; socialise with specifies the people involved.

items.pt: falar de assuntos de trabalho fora do expediente
items.section: A · Colleagues
items.example: We agreed not to talk shop during the weekend trip.
items.note: Informal idiom: discuss professional topics in a social setting.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Automating mundane checks freed the team to investigate harder faults.
items.note: Often describes dull everyday tasks; it does not necessarily imply poor quality.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The developers reorganised their tasks to meet the revised deadline.
items.note: Meet a deadline means finish on time; miss a deadline means fail to do so.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Two technicians volunteered for the overnight maintenance shift.
items.note: Volunteer for a task or volunteer to do something; do not confuse it with being assigned.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Mentoring new engineers can be demanding but extremely rewarding.
items.note: Highlights personal satisfaction or a sense of value, not necessarily financial reward.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The laboratory offered a stimulating environment for early-career researchers.
items.note: Typically evokes intellectual engagement or the generation of ideas.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Her heavy workload left little time for long-term planning.
items.note: Use heavy or light with workload; workload is the quantity of work assigned.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: During the holiday period, the support team had a relatively light workload.
items.note: Opposite of heavy workload; light is not a comment on task quality.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: She works the day shift when the laboratory is fully staffed.
items.note: Contrast with night shift; on the day shift is idiomatic.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The night shift detected an intermittent fault that the daytime team had missed.
items.note: Common prepositions are work the night shift or be on the night shift.

items.pt: automático e sem exigir reflexão; mecânico
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: After several months, the administrative routine became mechanical.
items.note: In a job description, mechanical can mean performed without much thought, not related to machinery.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The repetitive inspection procedure was eventually automated.
items.note: Repeated in a very similar way; often describes tedious tasks.

items.pt: encerrar o expediente; sair do trabalho
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: We usually knock off at half past five on Fridays.
items.note: Informal British phrasal verb; it can have other meanings in different contexts.

items.pt: monótono; cansativo pela falta de variedade
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The operator found the same monitoring routine monotonous after a few weeks.
items.note: Implies tedious sameness rather than sheer difficulty.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: It was satisfying to see the prototype pass its final tests.
items.note: Satisfying refers to the sense of fulfilment produced by the activity.

items.pt: desafiador; que exige esforço e habilidade
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The integration task was challenging but ultimately achievable.
items.note: Can be positively engaging, unlike monotonous or mind-numbing.

items.pt: glamouroso; visto como atraente e prestigiado
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The glamorous image of international travel conceals exhausting routines.
items.note: Often reflects an attractive public image rather than actual working conditions.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Emergency engineers often work irregular hours when incidents arise.
items.note: Times vary rather than following a fixed daily schedule.

items.pt: horários de trabalho que dificultam o convívio social
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Working antisocial hours makes it hard to attend family events.
items.note: British English term for shifts at evenings, nights or weekends; anti-social is also seen.

items.pt: preso a uma mesa de escritório
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: He switched to field engineering because he disliked being stuck behind a desk.
items.note: Informal: having to spend most of the working day at a desk.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Repeated long-haul flights eventually disrupted her sleeping routine.
items.note: Long-haul refers to routes covering long distances; short-haul is the opposite.

items.pt: entorpecente de tão monótono; extremamente tedioso
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Copying measurements by hand became a mind-numbing task.
items.note: Stronger than boring or monotonous; often suggests mental exhaustion.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The team had to work to a tight schedule before the accelerator shutdown.
items.note: Tight signals very little spare time or flexibility.

items.pt: trabalhar sob um cronograma muito apertado
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Construction crews are working to a tight schedule ahead of opening day.
items.note: Work to a schedule means follow it; the preposition to is idiomatic.

items.pt: preso a uma rotina sem perspectivas de mudança
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: She felt stuck in a rut and asked to take on a new project.
items.note: Idiom for an unchanging, unsatisfying pattern; often with feel or be.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: He left a dead-end job to retrain as an electrician.
items.note: A position with few or no prospects for promotion; normally hyphenated before job.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The technician calibrated the sensor before the experiment began.
items.note: Often a practical specialist who works with equipment and systems.

items.pt: requalificação profissional; formação para mudar de função
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: Retraining helped displaced employees move into new technical roles.
items.note: Training again, usually for a different occupation or changed requirements.

items.pt: associar-se a alguém em um empreendimento
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: She went in with a colleague to establish a small design consultancy.
items.note: Informal phrase for entering a business partnership; past tense went in with.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The start-up developed a low-cost instrument for university laboratories.
items.note: A recently established business, often innovative; typically a countable noun.

items.pt: autônomo; que trabalha por conta própria
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: After years as an employee, he became self-employed.
items.note: Describes employment status; self-employed people may work for one or many clients.

items.pt: freelancer; profissional que presta serviços a diferentes clientes
items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: She works freelance for several engineering consultancies.
items.note: Often describes project-based work for different clients; not synonymous in every context with self-employed.

items.section: B · During the day (different work patterns)
items.example: The computer programmer wrote scripts to automate equipment checks.
items.note: A professional who writes computer programs; programmer can also occur alone.

items.section: Exercises 5.1–5.4
items.example: Her role is varied, combining training, analysis and equipment maintenance.
items.note: Describes a range of different tasks; a positive contrast to repetitive work.

items.section: Exercises 5.1–5.4
items.example: Coordinating the emergency repair was stressful despite the experienced team.
items.note: Often describes activities that cause sustained pressure.

units.title: Unit 06 — At work: job satisfaction
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 18–19 (PDF pages 20–21).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Work and study · job satisfaction, remuneration and employment conditions
learningObjectives: Discuss job satisfaction, morale, stability and work–life balance with advanced workplace terminology.
Distinguish fast-moving and dynamic fields and use the patterns look to work in and seek a career in accurately.
Compare salary increments, bonuses, performance-linked rises, employment benefits and different categories of leave.
Explain voluntary versus compulsory redundancy and other workplace conditions using suitable register.

sectionsChecked: A · Aspects of job satisfaction, definitions and Language help box
B · Expressions connected with working life: leave, pay, benefits and redundancies

items.pt: satisfação profissional; realização com o trabalho
items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: Autonomy and meaningful responsibilities have improved job satisfaction across the team.
items.note: Refers to how fulfilled someone feels by their work, beyond pay alone.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: The company is trying to build a more inclusive workplace.
items.note: Can mean both the physical place and the working environment.

items.pt: comum; banal; sem nada de especial
items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: The assignment seemed run-of-the-mill until the team discovered a critical fault.
items.note: Informal expression for something ordinary, not necessarily poor in quality.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: Staff were no longer willing to put up with constant last-minute changes.
items.note: Phrasal verb followed by a noun or -ing form; implies tolerating something unwelcome.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: Short-term financial gains should not override long-term safety goals.
items.note: Contrast with long-term; both are normally hyphenated before nouns.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: The department invested in long-term staff development.
items.note: Frequently modifies plans, prospects, benefits and stability.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: For some applicants, financial reward matters less than professional autonomy.
items.note: Money received as a benefit or result; not synonymous with the psychological sense of rewarding.

items.pt: moral da equipe; ânimo dos funcionários
items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: Transparent management decisions helped rebuild staff morale.
items.note: Morale is collective confidence and enthusiasm; do not confuse it with morals.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: The board introduced a freeze on pay rises during the restructuring.
items.note: A freeze on something suspends it; pay rises is standard British English.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: Successful teamwork depends on clear responsibilities and mutual trust.
items.note: Usually uncountable; team work is less standard for this general concept.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: After two layoffs, job stability became her main priority.
items.note: Emphasises continuity and predictability of employment, not fulfilment.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: He decided against a high-risk career with uncertain income.
items.note: The nature of the risk depends on context: physical danger, finances or professional uncertainty.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: Regulation evolves quickly in fast-moving technology sectors.
items.note: Common with industries and markets; overlaps with dynamic but stresses speed of change.

items.pt: equilíbrio entre vida profissional e pessoal
items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: A flexible timetable helped her achieve a healthier work–life balance.
items.note: Balance between job demands and personal life; a compound noun with life.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: Graduates are attracted to dynamic workplaces with opportunities to innovate.
items.note: Suggests active development and change; not necessarily the same as a hectic workplace.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: Unclear promotion criteria left several employees feeling demotivated.
items.note: A state of reduced enthusiasm; demotivating describes the cause.

items.pt: buscar uma carreira em determinada área
items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: He decided to seek a career in renewable-energy engineering.
items.note: Formal alternative to look to work in a field; seek is typically followed by a direct object.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: After graduation, she is looking to work in medical robotics.
items.note: Look to do something means consider or plan it; not interchangeable with look for in this structure.

items.section: A · Aspects of job satisfaction
items.example: She has been looking for a job with more opportunities for training.
items.note: Look for means search for something; compare look to do something, meaning intend.

items.pt: perspectivas de carreira a longo prazo
items.section: Exercises 6.1–6.4
items.example: The role offered strong long-term career prospects despite the modest initial salary.
items.note: Career prospects refer to expected future opportunities, especially promotion or progression.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: She arranged maternity leave well before her expected delivery date.
items.note: Leave connected with childbirth; legal entitlement varies by country.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The new policy allows fathers to take paternity leave after a birth.
items.note: Leave for a father or second parent after childbirth; rules vary by jurisdiction.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: They applied for adoption leave after adopting a young child.
items.note: Leave to care for a newly adopted child; eligibility is jurisdiction-dependent.

items.pt: benefício extra; vantagem adicional no emprego
items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: One perk of the position is free access to professional training.
items.note: Informal, countable, normally used in the plural for job benefits.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The offer included employee benefits beyond the basic salary.
items.note: More neutral or formal than perks; may include insurance or paid leave.

items.pt: direito a dias de férias; quantidade de férias prevista
items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The contract specifies annual holiday entitlement in working days.
items.note: British English; a legal or contractual right to paid or unpaid time off.

items.pt: aumento salarial periódico; reajuste de salário
items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: Eligible staff receive a salary increment after a formal review.
items.note: Formal expression for an increase, often regular; it need not depend on performance.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: A performance-related pay rise rewarded the engineer for exceptional results.
items.note: An increase tied explicitly to individual or measured performance, unlike an automatic increment.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The company paid an annual bonus after exceeding its revenue target.
items.note: Extra payment once a year; distinct from a permanent increase to base pay.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: Several overworked employees requested a more realistic delivery schedule.
items.note: Overworked concerns excessive workload, not necessarily low salary.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: Employees argued that they were underpaid for their responsibilities.
items.note: Underpaid concerns pay considered too low for the work or market.

items.pt: sobrecarregado de trabalho e mal remunerado
items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The technicians joked that they were overworked and underpaid.
items.note: Conventional informal pairing, often humorous or used to criticise working conditions.

items.pt: desligamento por adesão voluntária a um programa de redução de pessoal
items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: Several senior employees chose voluntary redundancy under the new scheme.
items.note: In British employment English, an employee agrees to leave as part of downsizing; not simply resigning.

items.pt: demissão involuntária por extinção de posto de trabalho
items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The firm announced compulsory redundancies after closing the factory.
items.note: British term: roles are eliminated and employees have no choice; compare voluntary redundancy.

items.pt: equipe mínima necessária para manter a operação
items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The hospital continued operating with a skeleton staff during the strike.
items.note: A minimum complement of workers; staff is usually collective and uncountable here.

items.pt: banca de entrevistadores; grupo que conduz a entrevista de emprego
items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The interview panel included the technical manager and two senior researchers.
items.note: A group interviewing a candidate; also appears in recruitment contexts.

items.section: Exercises 6.1–6.4
items.example: Both parents qualified for parental leave under the revised policy.
items.note: Umbrella concept for parental absence from work; mentioned as an alternative in the answer key.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: The contract included health insurance and disability coverage.
items.note: Employee benefit; insurance coverage and entitlement differ by country.

items.section: B · Expressions connected with working life
items.example: A company car was provided because the role involved frequent site visits.
items.note: An employer-provided vehicle; may be considered a perk or benefit.
